blocks.text: The previous lesson covered requests in depth, this one covers the other half of every exchange, responses. A response is how a server answers a request, always tied back to that exact request by id, and always containing either a successful result or a clear error, never both, never neither.
1. The Three Parts of a Response

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: jsonrpc, id, and result or error make up a response

blocks.text: A response has a jsonrpc field marking the protocol version, the same id as the request it is answering, and either a result field, on success, or an error field, on failure, exactly one of those two, never both together.

blocks.title: A quick way to remember
blocks.content: Same id as always, then exactly one of two things, a result you can use or an error you need to handle.

blocks.text: Just like requests, the low-level details of assembling a response are usually handled by an SDK on the server side, a developer implementing a tool handler mostly just returns a plain value or raises an error.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can immediately say whether a given response is a success or a failure just by looking at which field is present, you have this concept down.

blocks.text: Once this shape feels automatic, reading a raw network trace of an MCP session becomes almost as easy as reading well-written prose.
2. The id Ties a Response to Its Request

A response is only meaningful in relation to the specific request it answers, the id is what makes that relationship explicit and checkable, a client receiving a response looks up which pending request shares that same id and resolves it with whatever the response contains.
Without this id-based link, a client receiving several responses close together would have no reliable way to know which request each one actually answers.
This same id-based matching is exactly what makes it safe for a client to send several requests without waiting for each one to finish before sending the next.

It also means clients written in entirely different programming languages, or maintained by entirely different teams, can still interoperate correctly, since the matching rule is part of the shared protocol, not any one implementation.
3. A Successful Response Carries a result

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A successful response carries a result field

blocks.text: When a request is fulfilled successfully, the response carries a result field, whose shape depends entirely on which method was called, a tools/call result looks different from a resources/read result, just as their corresponding request params differed.

The result for a given method should stay consistent in shape across calls, a client relying on a specific structure should not need to handle a completely different shape on a later call to the same method.
Documenting the expected result shape for each of your own server tools, right alongside its inputSchema, saves a lot of guesswork for anyone building a client against it later.
Even a simple confirmation result benefits from including a small, useful detail rather than an empty object, mirroring the same rich-results principle covered for tools earlier in this module.
4. A Failed Response Carries an error

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A failed response carries an error field

blocks.text: When a request cannot be fulfilled, the response carries an error field instead, containing at minimum a code and a message describing what went wrong, covered in full depth in the Error Responses lesson in the Communication Protocol module.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["code","A short, machine-readable identifier for the failure type"],["message","A human-readable explanation"]]}

code.content:
# a few common error codes seen across MCP servers
error_codes = ["invalid_arguments", "not_found", "unauthorized", "internal_error"]

blocks.title: A useful habit
blocks.content: Designing a small, consistent set of error codes for your own server, rather than inventing a new one for every possible failure, makes client-side error handling much simpler to write.

blocks.text: 5. result and error Are Mutually Exclusive

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: result and error never both appear

blocks.text: A response never contains both a result and an error at the same time, this strict either-or shape removes any ambiguity about whether a request succeeded, a client only ever needs to check for the presence of one or the other.
This strict rule simplifies client code considerably, a single if-else check, does this have an error, is enough to correctly branch between success and failure handling.

code.content:
# validating this rule directly
def is_valid_response(resp):
    has_result = "result" in resp
    has_error = "error" in resp
    return has_result != has_error   # exactly one, never both, never neither

blocks.text: Some early implementations of similar protocols allowed more ambiguous shapes, and the resulting confusion is a large part of why MCP enforces this strict either-or rule so consistently.
6. Matching Responses to Requests in Practice

A client typically keeps a lookup of pending requests keyed by id, when a response arrives, it looks up that id, resolves the pending request with the result or error, and removes it from the pending lookup.
This same pending-lookup pattern is exactly what most official MCP client SDKs implement internally, a developer using the SDK rarely has to write this matching logic by hand.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["1","Send request, store a pending entry keyed by id"],["2","Receive response"],["3","Look up and resolve the pending entry by id"]]}

blocks.text: Keeping this pending lookup bounded, clearing out entries that have already timed out, prevents a long-running client from slowly accumulating memory over time.
This same pattern generalizes cleanly beyond MCP itself, it is the standard way any request based protocol handles concurrent, asynchronous replies.
7. Responses Can Arrive Out of Order

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Response A with id 2 can arrive before response B with id 1

blocks.text: If several requests are in flight at once, their responses are not guaranteed to arrive in the same order the requests were sent, this is exactly why id-based matching matters so much, order alone is not a reliable way to pair them up.

code.content:
# two requests sent close together, responses arriving in reverse order
send_request(1, "tools/list")
send_request(2, "resources/list")
# response for id 2 might arrive before response for id 1, and that is fine

blocks.title: Why this happens
blocks.content: Different requests may take different amounts of time to process on the server side, a fast lookup can easily finish before a slower one that was sent moments earlier.

blocks.title: A related concurrency detail
blocks.content: This is exactly the same behavior discussed in the Requests lesson, from the sender side, this lesson simply covers what happens on the receiving end once those responses actually show up.

blocks.text: 8. A Response Is Never Sent for a Notification

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A notification gets no response sent

blocks.text: Since a notification has no id and expects nothing back, there is no such thing as a response to a notification, only requests receive responses, this is a direct consequence of the id-based matching covered throughout this lesson.
If a server mistakenly sends a response to something that was actually a notification, a well-behaved client should simply ignore it, since there was no pending request expecting a reply.

This asymmetry between requests and notifications is a small detail with a real consequence, code written to expect a response for every outgoing message will break the moment it sends a notification instead.
9. Timeouts and Missing Responses

If a response never arrives, due to a dropped connection or a server that crashed mid-request, a client needs its own timeout logic to eventually give up waiting, rather than leaving a pending request unresolved forever.

blocks.title: A practical pattern
blocks.content: A client can pair a timeout with automatic cleanup, removing the abandoned pending request from its lookup table so it does not leak memory over a long-running session.

blocks.text: A reasonable timeout duration often depends on the specific method being called, a quick lookup might warrant a short timeout, while a known slow operation warrants a longer one.

code.content:
# a timeout wrapped around a pending request
import asyncio
try:
    result = await asyncio.wait_for(pending[request_id], timeout=30)
except asyncio.TimeoutError:
    del pending[request_id]
    raise RuntimeError("Request timed out")

blocks.text: 10. Responses in Error-Handling Flows

An error response is not a failure of the protocol itself, it is a normal, expected outcome the protocol explicitly supports, a well-designed client treats an error response as useful information to act on, not as an exceptional case to be avoided.

This reframing matters especially for AI agents, a model that receives a clear error response can often recover gracefully, rephrasing its request or trying an alternative approach, rather than the whole interaction simply failing.
Some hosts even translate a common error code into a friendly, specific message shown to the end user, rather than surfacing the raw technical error text directly.
Designing error messages with the eventual reader in mind, whether that is a developer, a model, or an end user, is a small habit that pays off across every server you build.
11. Partial Results and Streaming Responses

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Partial result 1 and partial result 2 lead to a final result

blocks.text: Some operations, especially long-running ones, may deliver partial progress before a final response, this pattern, covered fully in the Streaming lesson in the Communication Protocol module, typically uses notifications to carry incremental updates, with the final response still arriving as the single, definitive answer.
This is one of the more advanced patterns in MCP, and it is worth returning to once the Notifications and Streaming lessons have both been covered in full.
12. Logging Responses Alongside Requests

Pairing every logged request with its corresponding logged response, matched by id, gives a complete before-and-after picture that is invaluable when diagnosing why a particular call did not behave as expected.
Some teams build lightweight internal tools specifically to replay a logged request-response pair for debugging, without needing to reconnect to the original live server.

code.content:
# a simple structured log entry pairing request and response
log.info({"id": 4, "method": "tools/call", "request": request, "response": response})

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Trace a request and its two possible outcomes, a successful response and a failed one, for the exact same original request.
Notice both possible responses share the exact same id, 4, confirming they both answer the exact same original request, only their outcome differs.
14. Common Mistakes When Working With Responses

items: Checking only for the presence of result without also handling the case where error is present instead.
Assuming responses arrive in the same order their requests were sent, and matching them by arrival order rather than id.
Expecting a response to a notification, which by definition never comes.
Never implementing a timeout, leaving a client waiting forever if a response is lost.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is logging only the request, and never the corresponding response, losing half of the information needed to understand what actually happened.
A sixth common mistake is swallowing an error response silently, logging nothing and simply returning None, making a real failure invisible until much later.
15. Practice: Write Your Own Response Handler
Write a small function that takes a response object and returns either the result or raises an error with the message from the error field, correctly distinguishing between the two cases.
Extend this handler to also log a warning whenever a response arrives with an id that does not match any currently pending request, a sign something unexpected has happened.
Try extending your handler further to retry automatically, once, on a specific transient error code, while immediately raising on any other error type.
Key Takeaway

A response always carries the same id as its request, along with exactly one of a result or an error, this simple, strict shape is what lets a client reliably match replies to requests, handle failures gracefully, and remain correct even when several requests are in flight concurrently.

With both requests and responses now covered in depth, the next lesson, Capabilities, looks at how client and server agree on what they each support in the first place, before any of these requests and responses can safely be exchanged.

The partial-results concept from the newly added section is worth remembering once you reach the Streaming lesson, since it shows how notifications and responses can work together for operations that take real time to complete.
